blocks.prompt: The Baby That Falls Out of the Sky
blocks.text: A giraffe is born by falling. Its mom stands up to give birth, and the baby drops about six feet to the ground. That is a hard landing. But the baby giraffe gets up in under an hour. By the end of the day, it can run. A baby giraffe is already taller than most grown people. It has two little horns on its head. They are called ossicones. They lie flat when the baby is born, so they do not hurt the mom on the way out. Then, after a few days, they stand up.

blocks.prompt: Seven Bones
blocks.text: A giraffe's neck is about six feet long. That is taller than most adults. So how many bones are inside it? You might guess fifty. The answer is seven. You have seven bones in your neck too. A giraffe's are just enormous. Each one can be as long as your forearm. Those seven bones make the giraffe the tallest animal on Earth. A big male can reach almost nineteen feet. He eats leaves that no other animal can reach, which means he almost never has to share his food. But the long neck causes a problem. When a giraffe wants a drink, it cannot bend its neck down to the water. Its neck is long, but its legs are longer. So it has to slide its front feet apart and lower itself, slowly, like a folding chair. For a few seconds it is stuck down there. A lion knows this. That is why giraffes drink fast, and why they would rather get their water out of wet leaves and skip the pond.

notes: Favorite food: the thorny acacia tree

blocks.prompt: The Trees Fight Back
blocks.text: A giraffe spends most of its day eating leaves, and its favorite tree is the acacia. The acacia does not agree to this arrangement. The first defense is thorns. Acacia branches are armed with spikes, some as long as your finger. The giraffe does not seem to care. Its tongue is about eighteen inches long and tough as a work glove, coated in thick saliva that lets it slide around the spikes and strip the leaves out from between them. So the tree tries something cleverer. Within minutes of a giraffe starting to feed, the acacia floods its leaves with bitter chemicals called tannins. The leaves turn foul. In large amounts, tannins can make an animal sick. The giraffe usually quits that tree after a few minutes and moves on. Here is the strange part. The wounded tree also releases a gas called ethylene into the air. Nearby acacias pick it up and start making tannins of their own, before a giraffe has even touched them. Researchers in South Africa noticed that giraffes rarely feed on two neighboring trees in a row. Instead they skip ahead, or they walk into the wind, where the warning gas has not traveled. So an animal that could eat whatever it wanted is being steered around the savanna by trees that cannot move, cannot see, and have no brain at all. The giraffe is not just tall. It is careful.

notes: The brain sits about six feet above the heart

blocks.prompt: The Plumbing Problem
blocks.text: Think about what it takes to be eighteen feet tall. Not the eating, not the walking. The plumbing. A giraffe's brain sits about six feet above its heart. To push blood that high against gravity, the giraffe runs a blood pressure roughly twice that of a healthy human, around 220 over 180. In a person, numbers like those would be a medical emergency. In a giraffe, they are an ordinary Tuesday. The pump behind them is a heart weighing about twenty-five pounds, with a left ventricle wall several inches thick, built like a muscular fist. That solves the problem of getting blood up. It creates the problem of getting blood back down. Blood in the legs of a tall animal should pool under its own weight until the skin swells and splits. It does not, because giraffe legs are wrapped in skin so tight and fibrous that scientists compare it to the compression stockings pilots and astronauts wear. The skin squeezes inward and holds the pressure in. Then there is the drinking problem. When a giraffe splays its legs and drops its head eight feet to reach water, all that pressure aims straight at its brain. Nothing about that should end well. Two things save it. The jugular veins in the neck carry one-way valves that snap shut and stop blood from running backward into the skull. And at the base of the brain sits a dense sponge of tiny branching vessels called the rete mirabile, Latin for wonderful net, which spreads the surge out and softens it before it arrives. When the giraffe snaps its head up again, the same system keeps the blood from draining away and dropping it in a faint. None of this was designed. Each piece is a repair for a problem the previous piece caused. Getting taller let giraffes reach food nothing else could reach, and every inch of that advantage had to be paid for somewhere else in the body. A giraffe is not simply a tall animal. It is a tall animal's worth of solutions, stacked on top of each other, walking around the savanna eating leaves.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Giraffa camelopardalis: the camel-leopard
Wild numbers fell about 40 percent in 30 years
Fewer giraffes in Africa than elephants
2016 genetics proposed four species, not one
Coat patches are inherited from the mother
Giraffes hum near 92 hertz at night

blocks.prompt: The Silent Extinction
blocks.text: Everyone knows the giraffe. It is on the alphabet poster, the nursery wall, the zoo map, the cartoon. It is one of the most recognizable animals on Earth, which turns out to be exactly the problem. Between the late 1980s and the 2010s, the wild giraffe population fell by roughly forty percent, from about 155,000 animals to under 100,000. Conservationists gave the collapse a name: the silent extinction. Silent, because almost nobody noticed. Elephants and rhinos have poaching crises with photographs attached, and the photographs made the news. The giraffe simply thinned out. Habitat was cleared for farmland, herds were cut into fragments too small to mix, conflict pushed hunting into the last strongholds, and a familiar animal quietly stopped being common. Until 2016, the giraffe was not even listed as threatened. There are now fewer giraffes in Africa than elephants, a sentence almost nobody would guess is true. The science was not paying close attention either. For most of the last century, every giraffe on the continent was filed as a single species, Giraffa camelopardalis, the camel-leopard, with a handful of subspecies sorted mainly by coat pattern. Then, in 2016, a team led by Julian Fennessy published a genetic survey of around two hundred giraffes and reported something nobody expected: the major groups had not interbred for perhaps a million years. They proposed four separate species. Some researchers accept that reading, some argue the data supports fewer, and the question is not settled. But the stakes are not academic. A population of 100,000 spread across one species sounds stable. That same population split four ways contains groups counted in the tens of thousands and one, the northern giraffe, with fewer than six thousand animals left. The same animals, counted differently, become an emergency. It matters that we misread them, because giraffes are stranger than their reputation. Males settle disputes by necking, swinging their skulls at each other like slow wrecking balls, and the bone of an adult male's head keeps thickening throughout his life to survive it. Their coat patches are unique to each animal, like fingerprints, and calves inherit the shape of their mother's spots. Underneath each patch runs a network of blood vessels that researchers think works as a thermal window, dumping heat. And for a long time people said giraffes were mute. In 2015, researchers at the University of Vienna recorded nearly a thousand hours of giraffes across three zoos and found that was wrong. At night, the giraffes hum, a low sound near ninety-two hertz, quiet enough that generations of keepers had walked past it. Nobody yet knows what the humming is for. That is the honest shape of the thing. We put this animal on the wall of every nursery in the world and never learned how many kinds of it there were, or that it talks at night. Fame is not the same as attention. The giraffe was hiding in plain sight, at eighteen feet tall, and we managed to lose almost half of them without looking up.
